Adult Live sharksuckers (Echeneis naucrates) attain a considerable ultimate total length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters], a size that positions them among the larger members of the Echeneidae family. This maximum dimension is typically recorded in large, presumably senescent individuals that have completed their somatic growth trajectory. The species exhibits a distinctive, laterally compressed body form and a highly modified dorsal fin that has evolved into a specialized adhesive disc, an adaptation for attaching to large marine vertebrates such as sharks, sea turtles, and rays. Field surveys and capture records from the tropical Atlantic and Indo-Pacific indicate that individuals of this size are relatively uncommon, suggesting that most adults in the population are smaller, perhaps due to the energetic demands of their commensal lifestyle. The elongated body shape and relatively modest mass for such a length reflect the species' streamlined morphology, which is well suited for rapid attachment and brief bursts of swimming alongside their mobile hosts.

In contrast to the maximum size, puberty in the Live sharksucker is attained at a total length of 40 centimeters [Lp = 40 centimeters]. This length-based threshold for the onset of gonadal maturation is derived from observed age-at-puberty estimates of approximately three to five years, combined with growth trajectory data. Reaching this size marks a significant life-history transition, after which individuals redirect resources from somatic growth toward reproductive development. Females become capable of vitellogenesis and males initiate spermatogenesis at this length, though first successful spawning may be deferred slightly as the fish continues to build energy reserves. The length-based metric is particularly useful for this species because size, rather than chronological age per se, is often the more reliable predictor of reproductive readiness in tropical marine fishes, where growth rates can vary considerably with food availability and host-association patterns. Available length-frequency distributions from capture records support 40 centimeters as a robust estimate for the onset of sexual maturation.

At a stable water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the estimated annual reproductive output of the Live sharksucker ranges from 10,192 to 42,151 eggs per year [Ri = 10,192 to 42,151 eggs per year], reflecting the species' batch-spawning strategy typical of many pelagic teleosts. This reproductive mode involves the release of multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season, with individual spawning events occurring at intervals of several days. The relatively high fecundity characterizes many pelagic-spawning teleosts, offsetting high rates of egg and larval mortality in the plankton. This iteroparous, batch-spawning mode allows females to spread reproductive effort across the season, buffering against stochastic environmental variation. The 27.2 °C thermal regime represents the average sea surface temperature encountered across much of the species' tropical range during the peak spawning months.

The wet weight of newly hatched Live sharksucker larvae is exceptionally low, estimated at 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], a value derived from the observed egg diameter range of 1,040 to 1,623 micrometers. Assuming a spherical egg with a mean diameter of approximately 1.3 millimeters, the calculated volume translates to this minute hatchling mass, which reflects the limited yolk reserves available to support the yolk-sac larva prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is brief, typically lasting only a few days before the mouth opens and the larva must commence feeding on small planktonic prey. The small size at hatching places the newly emerged larvae within the ichthyoplankton community, where they are subject to intense predation pressure. This life-history trait is consistent with a strategy of producing numerous, small offspring rather than fewer, larger ones, a pattern common among pelagic-spawning marine fishes that do not provide parental care. The diminutive larval size also constrains the initial gape and thus the size spectrum of available first prey items.

The maximum lifespan of the Live sharksucker is approximately eleven years [am = approximately eleven years], a duration that supports multiple reproductive seasons under the 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] thermal regime typical of its tropical habitat. This longevity estimate is derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis, and it is relatively extended for a tropical teleost of this body size. The species' association with large, long-lived hosts may confer a degree of protection from predation, potentially contributing to this longer lifespan. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults is 2,300 grams [Wwi = 2,300 grams], a mass that is modest given the species' 110 centimeter length, reflecting its slender, elongated body form adapted for hydrodynamic efficiency during attachment. The combination of a moderate growth rate, extended reproductive lifespan spanning multiple years, and iteroparous spawning defines a life-history strategy well suited to the unpredictable pelagic environment.
